![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/5e1d4dbd07dbf4e7f06b5ef2dd01ae2ef5fa82f3a5a78fb470388fad8b18af1e.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point: 

$\,$ $x=-1.5$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1.5)$ | $-1.5$ | $(-1.5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ | $\text{no extr.}$ | $↗$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical point. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=-1.5,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/8bee8a231cdfe8d41cf35fa50d97806d511a9477a8c92db98b1be11b70676928.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-\infty ,-1.5)$ and is increasing $↗$ on $(-1.5,+\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes down to the left and up to the right of $x=-1.5.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is decreasing to the left of $x=-1.5$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)<0$, and, since it is increasing to the right of $x=-1.5$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0.$ So, $x=-1.5$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave down to concave up.

So, we can draw as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/89127ba4db33c1c2ca12ddac05eac1c7e5ebe6540519fda1b55600620c1369d7.png)

- Finally, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/20784e268300c461c4567092230df10423b96d26287fde67074bab6690c1342f.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
